newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain-Prices reel on USDA forecast.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain-Prices reel on USDA forecast.

text.p: Australian grain prices slumped last week in reaction to USDA forecasts of a big world grains crop for 1996/97.

Price falls, of A$10.00-A15.00 a tonne for cash wheat and other grains, followed months of sliding grains prices as Australia gradually realised it would not be alone in producing a big wheat crop this year.
The USDA 1996/97 forecast of a 580 million tonne world wheat crop and ending stocks of 117.43 million tonnes was more adverse for Australian wheat than generally expected.
Australian cash wheat prices mostly dropped by about A$12 a tonne to end the week on about A$169 for the benchmark Australian Standard White delivered Newcastle.
Sorghum and barley also lost ground heavily, with cash sorghum falling by about A$15 a tonne to A$180 Newcastle or A$185 Sydney delivery and barley falling by A$8-A$10 to about A$140.

The Australian Wheat Board's A$10 a tonne cut in its pool price for all wheat grades on Monday, bringing the ASW price back to A$205 a tonne, had been factored into the market, Guy Allen of GrainCorp said.
But the big surprise, the USDA report on Wednesday, was "extremely bearish", he said. Australian cash wheat ended the week trading "sloppy", he said.
Lower prices ended the activity drought in recent weeks in Australian grains markets, scaring farmers into selling but still failing to attract significant end-user buying.
Weaker sorghum prices were produced by increased producer and some trade selling during the week, Allen said.
The GrainCorp executive did not see any reason for a rally.
"We've seen a further weakening, we've seen buyers pull back for old crop and new crop barley and wheat," Peter Sniekers of New England Agricultural Traders said.

Conflicting views on whether the market would continue to fall revolved around the tight world stock situation, where any sign of frost was likely to lead to increased prices, and increased forecast production, he said.
"We're hoping that it's bottomed out," he said.
But there were almost daily changes in perceptions, he said.

Increased forecasts for Australia's 1996/97 wheat crop -- by the Australian Wheat Board to 19.0 million tonnes from 17.6 million tonnes and by USDA to 19.5 million tonnes from 17.5 million tonnes -- failed to impress the market.

Previous forecasts had been seen by most of the trade as too low for some time. New forecasts are still seen as conservative, although closer to perceived reality of about 20 million tonnes. The AWB's indicative price for new crop ASW wheat delivered Newcastle fell by A$9 to A$168 over the week.
Australian wheat futures fell over the week after rising ahead of the USDA figures.
The January 1997 settlement price rose to A$182 mid-week after Monday's A$179 but the USDA forecast knocked it back to A$176.50 on Thursday and further to A$174 on Friday.
A more active week on the SFE saw 106 futures contracts and 69 options traded. Call options outnumbered puts 49-to-20.
